$comment: §NEWLY-MEASURED (2026-08-12) — THE THIRD STATE. NOT DEBT. NOT A REGRESSION.
gate-debt.json declares exactly two states, and BIM 3.0 Phase 1 produces a third
one that fits neither:
• REGRESSION      — a gate fails and is NOT on gate-debt.json. Something got
WORSE. Blocks.
• DECLARED DEBT   — a gate is ON gate-debt.json. Somebody CHOSE to ship a known
contract violation (rule 3: never added without an explicit
founder/architect decision).
• NEWLY MEASURED  — THIS FILE. A gate that was BUILT THIS WEEK and lands RED on
defects that PREDATE it. Nothing got worse; the INSTRUMENT
ARRIVED. And nobody chose to ship these — they were never
measured, so there was no decision to make.
Filing a newly-measured gate under either existing label is a lie in a different
direction each way. Calling it a REGRESSION says the tree got worse on the day
someone wrote a scanner, which trains people to read red as noise — that is how
the whole suite ended up unwired in the first place (L-774). Calling it DECLARED
DEBT backdates a decision nobody made and quietly converts 'we have never looked
at this' into 'we accepted this', which is the §CONTEXT-DATA-HONESTY failure this
repository keeps paying for: two very different facts printing the same value.
─── WHY A SIBLING FILE AND NOT A SECTION INSIDE gate-debt.json ───────────────
Three reasons, in order of weight:
1. DIFFERENT CONSENT RULES. gate-debt.json rule 3 attaches a founder decision to
the ACT OF ADDING A LINE, because adding one there means choosing to ship a
known violation. This category's entries are the opposite act — choosing to
START MEASURING. Putting both under one roof means the strongest rule in that
file (rule 3) either leaks onto entries that should not need it, or gets
weakened to accommodate them. Rule 3 is left untouched and un-diluted by
keeping this out of that file entirely.
2. DIFFERENT SHAPE. gate-debt.json's `failing` is a bare `string[]` — a name and
nothing else. An entry here is meaningless without its pinned reading, its
exit condition and its review date. Bolting a structured array beside a flat
one in the same file gives readers of `failing` a partial view of what the
suite tolerates, which is exactly the shape of defect §3.20 K2 of
BIM30-READINESS-GATES names: one list that grows to fit whatever is failing.
3. TWO LISTS ARE AUDITABLE; ONE MERGED LIST IS NOT. The sizes of these two files
mean different things and must be readable separately. Declared debt going up
is bad news. This file going up is, on its face, GOOD news — it means more of
the estate is instrumented — right up until an entry expires unfixed.
─── DOES ADDING HERE NEED A FOUNDER DECISION? NO — WITH THREE HARD EDGES ─────
STATED EXPLICITLY BECAUSE THE ANSWER DIFFERS FROM RULE 3 AND MUST NOT BE INFERRED.
Adding a FIRST READING for a gate does NOT require a founder decision. Requiring
one would put a human approval step in front of TURNING AN INSTRUMENT ON, and the
predictable response to that friction is to not land the gate — which is precisely
what BIM30-READINESS-GATES §2.3 forbids: *deferring a gate until its subject is
fixed is how a subject stays unfixed*. The founder's authority is over what we
SHIP, not over what we are ALLOWED TO KNOW. An entry here asserts no tolerance; it
asserts that a number has been written down and may now only fall.
The three edges, each of which IS a decision and therefore DOES need the founder:
(a) AN ENTRY MAY ONLY BE ADDED IN THE COMMIT THAT INTRODUCES ITS GATE. An entry
added later is not a first reading — the gate ran and something changed — so
it is either a regression or debt, and it goes through rule 3.
(b) RAISING A PINNED READING IS FORBIDDEN OUTRIGHT, founder or not. That is R7:
a measurement raised becomes a permission. The only legal edit to a reading
is downward.
(c) EXTENDING A `reviewBy`, OR MOVING AN ENTRY FROM THIS FILE TO gate-debt.json,
REQUIRES THE FOUNDER. That is the moment 'we have not fixed this yet' turns
into 'we are choosing to live with this', and it is exactly the decision
rule 3 exists to gate. This is the join between the two files, and it is
deliberately the only one.
─── THE RATCHET LIVES IN THE GATE, NOT IN THIS FILE ─────────────────────────
Every entry below is a gate that reports through the ONE exit-code implementation
at tools/rac-conformance/certification/contract.ts. That implementation already
returns 3 when findings exceed the declared level and 3 when a declared entry is
no longer measured. So:
exit 1 → at or below the pin. run-all absorbs it AS NEWLY-MEASURED.
exit 3 → the pin was exceeded, or the gate's own ledger is stale.
NEVER ABSORBED HERE. run-all's §RATCHET-EXCEEDED-IS-NEVER-DEBT branch
fires before this file is consulted, and it exits 1 for the suite.
This file therefore does NOT re-implement the ratchet, and must not: a second
comparator over the same number is a second thing that can disagree. `pinnedTo`
below is a POINTER to where the authoritative number lives plus a human-readable
copy of it — if the two ever disagree, THE GATE IS RIGHT and this file is stale.
─── TIME-BOUNDED, AND THE BOUND IS ENFORCED ─────────────────────────────────
Every entry carries `reviewBy`. run-all FAILS when today > reviewBy. That is the
whole point of the field: a category with no exit is how 'temporary' becomes
permanent, and a date nobody enforces is a comment. `reviewBy` is NOT a fix
deadline — it is the date by which the entry must be re-argued: fixed and struck,
or moved to gate-debt.json as an explicit founder decision to live with it. Both
outcomes are honest. Silently sitting here for a year is not.
─── PAID INSTRUMENT DEBT LEAVES THIS FILE TOO ───────────────────────────────
The gate-debt.json rule-2 discipline applies verbatim: an entry here whose gate
starts PASSING is a FAILURE of this file and run-all says so. Otherwise this rots
into a list of things that are secretly fine, which is the one failure mode both
ledgers share.
createdBecause: BIM 3.0 Phase 1 Tier 1 landed three gates RED on pre-existing production defects (BIM30-READINESS-GATES §2.3), and gate-debt.json had no category that described them without lying.
